strengths: Provides a genuine theoretical contribution (Theorem 1) deriving an approximation-error lower bound for unitary functions via group-invariance theory, giving a principled explanation for why strict unitary convolutions are overconstrained for dynamics with high angular dependence in solution norm (e.g., diffusion).

Non-trivial and carefully justified extension of the Rayleigh quotient and unitary convolution framework from graphs to meshes, correctly identifying and fixing the subtlety that raw cotangent weights can be negative (invalidating the Rayleigh quotient) and resolving this via the Robust Laplacian/Delaunay rewiring with a formal proof (Corollary 1) under a clearly stated assumption.

Two concrete, complementary relaxation mechanisms (Taylor truncation and encoder-decoder) are proposed with a clear rationale for when each is preferable, and a sensitivity analysis (Sec. B.2) supports the choice of truncation order.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation across a controlled motivating experiment (grid heat diffusion), multiple PDEs (heat, wave, Cahn-Hilliard) on complex real meshes, and a real-world weather forecasting benchmark (WB2/ERA5), compared against strong and diverse baselines (equivariant networks, mesh transformers, MPNNs).

The paper is honest about mixed results and limitations (e.g., admitting other models sometimes win on SMAPE/RE for wave and Cahn-Hilliard, and that WB2 performance is below SOTA due to compute constraints), and supplements the main Rayleigh-quotient metric with an independent, more global smoothness measure (2-point correlation function) that corroborates the main findings.
Extensive appendix with full proofs, dataset generation details, and additional diagnostics/ablations supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim of outperformance is strongest only for the heat equation; for wave and Cahn-Hilliard, R-UniMesh is frequently not the best method (e.g., GemCNN beats it on Cahn-Hilliard NRMSE, EMAN/Transformer have lower RE on wave), so the paper's framing as broadly "outperforming baselines" somewhat overstates a result that is really heat-diffusion-specific.

Several baselines (GCN, EGNN) fail to converge or perform very poorly across many settings (dashes in Table 2, extreme RMSE values in Table 7), raising questions about whether the tight ~40-50k parameter budget and training setup are fair to all methods, and undermining confidence that comparisons are apples-to-apples.

WB2 experiments use a reduced dataset/training budget and all models (including R-UniMesh) remain below SOTA performance, limiting the strength of claims about real-world applicability; compute-constrained comparisons make it hard to assess whether relative rankings would hold at scale.

No wall-clock time, memory, or FLOP comparison is provided between R-UniMesh/R-UniGraph and baselines, despite the matrix-exponential-based unitary/relaxed-unitary layers plausibly being more expensive; scalability of the approach is not empirically quantified.

Results are reported over a small number of test meshes per PDE with substantial variance (e.g., very large standard deviations for wave NRMSE), and there is no significance testing to establish that reported differences are statistically meaningful.

The theoretical result (Theorem 1), while a useful and correctly executed application, is largely a direct instantiation of an existing group-invariance error bound (Proposition 2 from Wang et al. 2023) rather than a fundamentally new proof technique, somewhat limiting the theoretical novelty.

Sensitivity/robustness analysis of the relaxation hyperparameters (Taylor truncation order, encoder depth) is only performed on the simple grid-graph motivating experiment and not extended to the more complex PyVista mesh or WB2 settings where it matters most for practitioners.

strengths: The core motivating idea—that unitary convolutions, while provably preserving the Rayleigh quotient, are over-constraining for naturally-smoothing dynamics like diffusion—is a clear and well-motivated observation that fills a real gap in the oversmoothing literature (Kiani et al., 2024).

Theorem 1 provides a principled (if somewhat abstract) approximation-error lower bound for unitary functions based on group-invariance theory (building on Wang et al., 2023), giving some formal grounding for why unitary constraints can hurt when the target's norm has high angular dependence.

The extension of the Rayleigh quotient and unitary/relaxed-unitary convolutions from graphs to triangular meshes, using the Robust Laplacian and intrinsic Delaunay rewiring to guarantee non-negative, symmetric cotangent weights, is a reasonably novel and non-trivial technical contribution, with a supporting proof (Corollary 1).

The controlled synthetic experiment (Sec. 6.1, heat diffusion on grid graphs) is clean and convincingly isolates the effect of Taylor-truncation relaxation versus full unitary and unconstrained GCN baselines, directly supporting the central hypothesis.

The empirical evaluation is broad, spanning synthetic PDEs (heat, wave, Cahn-Hilliard) on complex real-world meshes and a real-world weather forecasting benchmark (WeatherBench2), with a reasonably large set of baselines including gauge- and Euclidean-equivariant models and mesh transformers.

Useful supplementary analyses (Taylor truncation sensitivity, 2-point correlation smoothness metric, qualitative rollout comparisons) attempt to validate the proposed Rayleigh-quotient-based metric against more standard/global notions of smoothness.
weaknesses: A major experimental fairness concern: baselines GemCNN, EMAN, and Hermes are evaluated using pretrained checkpoints from Park et al. (2023), while the proposed R-UNIMESH and other baselines (GCN, Transformer, MPNN, EGNN) are freshly trained by the authors under a specific parameter/compute budget. This asymmetry in training protocol undermines the central claim that R-UNIMESH 'outperforms strong baselines,' since differences in training regime rather than architecture could explain performance gaps.

The claim of outperforming baselines is not uniformly supported by the reported numbers: on the Wave equation, R-UNIMESH has the worst SMAPE among all converging methods (385.2 vs. 301.0-327.0 for others), and on Cahn-Hilliard it is not best on any metric. The paper's narrative overstates the generality of the improvement, which appears largely confined to the heat/diffusion setting.

There is a significant gap between the theoretical result (Theorem 1, stated for single-channel functions u, f : C^n -> C^n) and the practical architectures used in experiments, which operate on multi-channel node features (X in C^{n x d}) and involve many layers, nonlinearities, and relaxation hyperparameters (Tmax, encoder-decoder depth) whose connection to the stated bound is only loosely argued via an empirical sensitivity analysis rather than a formal result tying Tmax to approximation error.

Many baseline models diverge or produce pathological results in the WeatherBench2 experiments (e.g., EMAN RMSE exceeding 10^9, GCN RMSE exceeding 10^14, Transformer with near-constant/negative ACC), suggesting inadequate baseline tuning or training instability rather than fundamental architectural limitations; this weakens confidence in the comparative conclusions drawn from this benchmark.

All WB2 models remain well below SOTA performance (Rasp et al., 2024) and are trained on a reduced dataset/resolution and compute budget, limiting the significance of the weather-forecasting results as evidence for real-world applicability.

The 40-50k parameter budget constraint (inherited from Park et al., 2023) is acknowledged to disadvantage non-unitary models that could scale better with more parameters, and it is unclear whether this budget is equally fair to unitary-constrained architectures versus flexible baselines, since unitary layers cannot change channel dimensionality (motivating the authors' own encoder-decoder relaxation) -- this could asymmetrically help or hurt different architectures.

The newly introduced Rayleigh Error (RE) metric and its correspondence to a more global 2-point correlation smoothness metric are validated only on a small number of qualitative examples (e.g., a single mesh, single equation), which is insufficient to establish RE as a reliable, generally applicable smoothness diagnostic.

Error bars are large relative to reported differences in several tables (e.g., Wave RE: 93.5 +/- 25.4 for R-UNIMESH vs. 73.57 +/- 6.5 for EMAN), and no statistical significance testing is provided, making some claimed rankings between methods appear within noise.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated central thesis: unitary convolutions strictly preserve the Rayleigh quotient, which is provably suboptimal when the target dynamics (e.g., diffusion) require smoothing/undersmoothing; this is a useful and underexplored critique that extends/complements Kiani et al. (2024).

A reasonably rigorous theoretical contribution (Theorem 1) deriving a lower bound on approximation error for unitary functions via group-invariance theory, giving formal justification for why unitary constraints can be overly restrictive when the target's norm has high angular dependence.

Non-trivial and carefully justified extension of the Rayleigh quotient and unitary/relaxed-unitary convolution framework from graphs to meshes, correctly handling the subtlety that cotangent weights can be negative (via the Robust Laplacian/Delaunay rewiring) with a supporting proof (Corollary 1).

Two concrete, well-motivated relaxation mechanisms (Taylor truncation and encoder-decoder) with complementary strengths (fine-grained control vs. parameter scalability), supported by a sensitivity analysis (Sec. B.2) showing that small truncation orders already achieve near-unitary behavior.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across a synthetic heat-diffusion task, several PDEs on complex real meshes (heat, wave, Cahn-Hilliard) with many strong baselines (GCN, MPNN, EGNN, GemCNN, EMAN, Hermes, mesh transformer), and a real-world large-scale benchmark (WeatherBench2), together with multiple complementary metrics (NRMSE, SMAPE, Rayleigh Error, and a beyond-1-hop 2-point correlation smoothness metric) and qualitative/video diagnostics that corroborate the quantitative claims.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim of consistent superiority is only strongly supported for the heat equation; on the wave and Cahn-Hilliard tasks (Table 2) R-UniMesh is not the best method on most metrics (e.g., worse SMAPE on wave, worse RE than Transformer/EMAN/Hermes on wave and CH), making the abstract's claim of outperforming baselines somewhat overstated relative to the full results.

On the real-world WeatherBench2 benchmark, the paper itself notes that 'the equivariant and unitary models show no significant advantage' and all models underperform SOTA, which weakens the paper's core narrative that explicit smoothness control is the key driver of performance in realistic settings.

Several baselines fail to converge entirely (dashes in Table 2) under the fixed ~40-50k parameter budget; it is unclear whether this reflects an intrinsic limitation of those architectures or an artifact of the restrictive, possibly baseline-unfriendly training budget, raising fairness-of-comparison concerns.

There is a theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 and the unitary preservation proofs are stated for complex unitary groups (U(n), SU(n)), whereas the actual R-UniMesh implementation uses real orthogonal weights for real-valued tasks; the paper does not explicitly reconcile how the complex-valued approximation bound transfers to the orthogonal/real setting used in experiments.

Error bars are large relative to reported differences in several tables (e.g., Cahn-Hilliard RE, WB2 RE for some variables), and no formal statistical significance testing is provided, making some claimed 'best' or 'competitive' results less conclusive.

The WB2 mesh construction is a simple lat-lon projection rather than more standard geodesic/icosahedral meshes used by strong operational baselines, and training data/model size are reduced from SOTA settings for compute reasons; while acknowledged, this limits the strength of conclusions drawn from the weather forecasting experiments.
